title: Grouping and capturing
summary: Parentheses do two jobs: they group a piece of a pattern, and they capture what it matched. Read captures in C# with Match.Groups, and group without capturing with (?:...).

steps.title: Parentheses do two jobs
body: A quantifier applies to the one thing just before it. `ab+` means an `a` and then one or more `b`. To repeat a
longer piece, wrap it in parentheses: `(ab)+` matches `ab`, `abab`, `ababab`.
Parentheses also **capture**: the engine remembers the text each group matched, so your code can read it
afterwards. That is how you pull fields out of a log line instead of only asking "does it match?".
| Pattern | Means |
| `ab+` | `a`, then one or more `b` |
| `(ab)+` | one or more `ab`, and group 1 remembers the last one |
| `(\w+)=(\d+)` | a key and a number; group 1 is the key, group 2 the number |
Below, every `key=number` pair is found, and each group is coloured. Try `(\w+)=` alone, then add the second group back.

steps.prompt: Which strings does `(ab)+` match the **whole** of? Select all that apply.
steps.explain: `(ab)+` repeats the pair `ab` one or more times. `abbb` is what `ab+` matches: there the `+` only repeats the `b`. `+` needs at least one repetition, so the empty string does not match.

steps.title: A three-part version number
prompt: Release tags use three numbers joined by dots: `1.2.3`, `10.0.14`. Match the **whole** string when it is
exactly that. Use a group with a quantifier for the repeated "dot and a number" part, instead of writing it twice.
Use `[0-9]`, not `\d` (remember the Unicode digits from module 1).
hints: The part that repeats is a dot followed by digits: `\.[0-9]+`.
`[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+){2}`: one number, then the group exactly twice.
steps.explain: `(\.[0-9]+){2}` repeats the whole group. Without the parentheses, a `{2}` would apply only to the single item just before it. The checks compare the whole string, so `1.2.3.4` is rejected.

steps.title: Reading captures in C#
body: `Regex.Match` returns the first match. Check `Success` first, then read the groups:
```csharp
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
var m = Regex.Match("09:12 status=503 in 1200ms", @"status=(\d{3}) in (\d+)ms");
if (m.Success)
Console.WriteLine(m.Groups[0].Value);   // status=503 in 1200ms  (the whole match)
Console.WriteLine(m.Groups[1].Value);   // 503
Console.WriteLine(m.Groups[2].Value);   // 1200
- Group 0 is always the whole match.
- Groups are numbered by their **opening** parenthesis, counted from the left. A group inside another group gets
the next number after its parent.
- `Value` is always a string. Convert it yourself (`int.Parse`), and only after checking `Success`: reading
`Groups[1]` of a failed match gives an empty string, and `int.Parse("")` throws.

steps.prompt: Groups are numbered by their opening parenthesis. What does this print?
steps.explain: Count the `(` from the left: `(\w+)` is 1, `(/\w+/(\d+))` opens second so it is 2, the `(\d+)` nested inside it opens third so it is 3, and the status is 4.

steps.title: Capture a config key and its value
prompt: A config file has lines like `timeout=30` and `max_retries=5`. Match the whole line, with the key (lowercase
letters and underscores) in **group 1** and the value (any characters except whitespace, at least one) in **group 2**.
hints: Two groups with a literal `=` between them.
steps.explain: Each pair of parentheses captures its part. `\S+` takes everything up to the first space, so a value like `eu-west-1` arrives whole.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a method that returns the status code from a line like `GET /pay status=503`, or `null` when there is none.
steps.explain: Match, check `Success`, then read the group. Parsing before the check would throw on a line without a status.

steps.title: Grouping without capturing: (?:...)
body: Often you need parentheses only to group: `(GET|POST)` so that `|` covers just the method, or `(\.[0-9]+){2}` so
that the quantifier covers a dot and digits. Writing `(?:...)` groups **without** capturing.
Why seniors prefer it when they do not need the text:
- **Stable numbering.** A non-capturing group takes no number, so the groups you do read keep their numbers.
- **Less work.** The engine does not record where the group started and ended on every attempt. In a hot loop
over a large log that is measurable.
- **Clear intent.** A reviewer sees at once which groups the code reads.
Below, the method is grouped but not captured, so the path is group 1.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so that `host` gets the host name of the URL. The scheme is grouped but must not take a group number.
steps.explain: `(?:http|https)` groups the alternatives without a number, so the host is group 1. Group 0 would be the whole match, and with a capturing scheme group the host would move to 2.

steps.title: Capture the host of a URL
prompt: Find a URL starting with `http://` or `https://` and capture its host in **group 1**. The host ends at a `/`,
a `:` (a port), a `?` or the end of the URL.
Group 1 must be the host, so the scheme must not be a capturing group: use `s?` or `(?:...)`.
`ftp://` URLs and bare host names do not count.
hints: The host is one or more characters that are not `/`, `:`, `?` or whitespace: `[^/:?\s]+`.
steps.explain: A negated class says where the host stops, which is clearer and faster than a lazy `.*?`. Writing `(https?)` would make the scheme group 1 and push the host to group 2.

steps.title: HostOf
prompt: Write `string? HostOf(string url)`. When `url` **starts with** `http://` or `https://`, return its host (it ends
at `/`, `:`, `?` or the end). Otherwise return `null`.
| `see https://x.contoso.com` | `null` (does not start with the scheme) |
Use `Regex.Match`, check `Success`, and read the host from `Groups`. `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("http URL with a port", "localhost", HostOf("http://localhost:5000/health"));
Dojo.Eq("URL that is only scheme and host", "contoso.com", HostOf("https://contoso.com"));
Dojo.Eq("must start with the scheme", (string?)null, HostOf("see https://x.contoso.com"));

require.message: Checks Success before reading the group

hints: Anchor the pattern with `^` and capture the host: `^https?://([^/:?]+)`.
